en: The Jātaka,
Great Section (Mahānipāta), Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
The Vidhura Jātaka, Chapter One:
The Section on the Craving “O pale one, you are emaciated and weak.”
"O knower of the Vedas, you who were previously renowned for your beauty and form—
being asked by me, O stainless one, tell me:
what is the nature of the bodily pain you experience?"
“O Lord of Men, among human beings, ‘dhamma’ is called the longing of pregnant women; O Elephant-like Naga,
[you have fulfilled] that which was longed for by dhamma.”
"O Vidhura, what is it that you long for in your heart?
"You long for the moon,
or perhaps the sun, or even the wind."
“Rare indeed is the sight of one who is a protector;
who here would honor such a protector?
“But why, dear father, do you brood so?”
Your face is like a lotus held in the hand;
why are you so dejected in appearance, O Lord?
Do not grieve, O scorcher of your enemies!
“Your mother, indeed, is grieving;
Vidhura’s heart is tormented.
For it is difficult to behold Vidhura again.”
"Who here will honor Vidhura?
Go in search of one who will honor Vidhura here."
Having heard her father’s words, she went out at night and behaved lustfully. [She asked:
“Who are the Gandhabbas, the Rakkhasas, and the Nāgas?”
"Who among the kinnaras or humans is wise,
one who can grant all desires,
and who will become my husband for a long time?"
“I shall be your comforter as your husband, I shall be your provider,
O lady of faultless eyes; for such is my wisdom.”
“You shall be my wife, Assāsa,” thus Irandhatī spoke to Puṇṇaka with a mind following its former path.
“Come, let us go into the presence of my father;
he himself will explain this matter to you.
Thus adorned and well-robed, they departed.
Mālinī, radiant with sandalwood paste,
took the yakkha by the hand and went into the presence of her father.
“O best of Nāgas, listen to my words;
act in a fitting and meritorious manner.
I long for Irandhatī.”
Endow me with that very thing.
A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
and a hundred chariots drawn by mules—
There are a hundred gables filled entirely with various jewels;
O Naga, enter into them.
"Give me your daughter, Randhatī.
"Wait while I inform my kinsmen,
friends, and well-wishers."
An action performed without consulting others leads to regret later.
Then that Naga Varuṇa—
Having entered the residence,
he addressed his wife and spoke these words.
“This is that yakkha Puṇṇaka,
who entreats me for Irandhatī in exchange for a great gain of wealth.”
“Let us give our beloved to him.
“Iranda, we cannot be obtained by wealth or by riches.”
But if the heart of the wise man,
having obtained it righteously here, should bring it forth—
by such wealth as this, O maiden, you may be won.
“We do not seek any other wealth beyond this.
Then that Naga Varuṇa,
having emerged from his dwelling;
Having caused Puṇṇaka to desire [him],
he spoke these words:
"Neither by wealth nor by riches..."
"Irandhatī can be obtained by us;
if you have affection for the wise man,
then having won her here according to the law, do not speak ill of her."
"With this wealth, the maiden can be obtained;
we do not seek any other wealth beyond this.
"He whom some in the world call 'wise'—"
Others, however, call that very same person a fool.
Tell me, O Naga, since they dispute here,
whom do you call a wise man?
“If Vidhura by name is the son of King Koravya Dhanañjaya the Wealth-Heap,
bring that wise man here, acquired through righteousness.”
"Let Irandhatī be your follower.
Having heard these words of Varuṇa,
the Yakkha arose, exceedingly joyful.
Right there, the wise man gave this instruction:
"Bring a well-bred horse harnessed right here;
its ears are made of gold."
The hooves are made of emerald,
and the breast-plate is of gold from the Jambū River, refined by smelting.
Puṇṇaka, having mounted a horse-drawn carriage that carried the gods,
was adorned and had his hair and beard trimmed.
He set out through the air into the sky.
That Puṇṇaka, greedy with sensual lust,
was seeking to win the Naga maiden Irandhatī.
Having gone to that illustrious lord of beings,
he spoke thus to Vessavaṇa Kuvera:
“In the palace named Bhogavatī, ...”
It was called Vāsā, the Golden One;
it was built in the city made of gold,
completed for the serpent Maṇḍalaka.
Towers with battlements and arched gateways,
made of ruby and cat’s-eye gemstone;
here are palaces constructed of stone.
It was covered with golden jewels.
There were mangoes, *tilaka* trees,
rose-apples, *sattapaṇṇa*, *mucalinda*, and *ketaka* trees.
Piyangu, uddālaka, and sahā;
uparibhaddaka and sinduvāraka;
campeyyaka and nāgamallikā.
Then the Koliyan women brought garlands for me here;
these trees, having been dedicated [to me],
beautify the abode of the Naga.
There are many stone and golden trees here that are perpetually in bloom; while dwelling there,
one is free from falling into pits.
The Naga king Varuṇa was of great psychic power.
His wife was Komārikā,
Vimalā, whose body was like a streak of refined gold.
Black, youthful, and tall,
with breasts like *pucimanda* fruits and lovely to behold,
her beautiful skin was as red as lac-dye.
Like *kaṇikāra* flowers blooming in a windless place,
like celestial nymphs wandering in the third heaven,
they were like lightning flashing forth from a thick cloud.
She, longing and greatly amazed,
yearns for Vidhura’s heart;
O Lord, I give that to them.
Therefore they gave me Irandhatī.
Then Puṇṇaka addressed the glorious lord of spirits, Vessavaṇa Kuvera:
“While staying right there, he addressed the man:
‘Bring a well-bred horse, harnessed right here.
His ears were made of gold.”
The hooves are made of emerald,
and the breastplate of the golden Jāmbūnada gold, as if it were ripe fruit.
Puṇṇaka, adorned and with his hair and beard trimmed, mounted a horse that was a vehicle for carrying the gods.
He set out through the sky, through the atmosphere.
He arrived at the most delightful Rājagaha,
the city of King Aṅga, which was difficult to assail.
Abounding in food and plentiful in drink,
like the abode of Vāsava at Masakkasāra,
it resounds with the cries of flocks of peacocks and herons.
Resounding with the cries of birds and frequented by flocks of winged creatures,
that beautiful grove, filled with the warbling of various birds and strewn with flowers, was like the Himavat mountain.
Thus Puṇṇaka ascended Mount Vepulla,
that mountain peak frequented by kimpurisas,
searching for a magnificent jewel-treasure.
He saw it in the midst of the mountain peak—
a brilliant, well-born jewel,
a magnificent and captivating gem of great value.
Shining with glory, that illustrious one illuminates like lightning in the sky.
He took hold of that precious beryl.
Mounting the majestic steed named Manohara,
he of mind-made form departed through the sky by way of the air.
Thus he reached the city of Indapattha and, having descended,
approached the assembly hall of the Kurus;
there one hundred and one kings had gathered together in harmony.
The yakṣa, unshakable, pierced through:
"Who here among kings attains the boon?
Whom shall we overcome with the wealth of boons?"
“We conquer the unsurpassed, most excellent jewel;
who indeed can conquer us with superior wealth?
“In what kingdom, then, is your native land?”
"This speech of yours is not like that of a Kauravya;
you are fearless before our splendor and appearance.
Tell me your name and your kinsmen."
“I am a young brahmin named Kaccāyana, O King;
they call me by my full name.
My kinsmen and relatives live among the Aṅgas.”
"O God, I have arrived here by means of a die.
"What treasures does this young man possess,
that the gambler, by defeating him, might carry them off?"
“The king possesses many jewels;
how can you, being poor, summon them?
“This jewel of mine is named Manohara.”
“The magnificent, mind-captivating jewel,
and this thoroughbred horse that torments his enemies—
having defeated me, let the gambler take these.”
“O young man, what will a single gem do?
And what will a single thoroughbred horse do?
A king possesses many precious gems.”
“Or there are many noble steeds, swift as the wind.
This concludes the Chapter on Longings.
2. The Chapter on Jewels.
“And this jewel-treasure of mine—
behold it, O Best of Bipeds—
herein are the forms of women.”
And the conflicts of men,
as well as the conflicts of wild beasts here,
and the conflicts of birds;
The king of nāgas and the supaṇṇas—
behold them fashioned upon the gem.
The elephant corps and the chariot corps.
Horsemen and armored foot soldiers—
behold this fourfold army fashioned within the jewel.
Elephant-riders stationed in the ranks,
charioteers, and infantrymen;
the elite forces were arrayed.
Behold the city fashioned within the gem, complete with lofty heights,
many walls, and arched gateways.
Behold the grounds fashioned from jewels in the courtyards,
as well as the pillars and the moats.
The door-panels and the bolts;
look at the watchtowers and the gate fashioned upon the gem.
Behold, on the paths to the archways,
many flocks of various birds:
swans, cranes, and peacocks.
Cakravāka ducks and kuṇāla birds,
many variegated ones,
crested peacocks, and jīvajīvaka birds;
Behold the city fashioned within the jewel, filled with various groups of beings, and surrounded by a magnificent wall.
Behold the city with its well-built ramparts.
It was wonderful and hair-raising,
with its banners raised high, delightful,
and strewn with golden sand.
Behold these leaf-huts,
divided and measured out in parts;
in dwellings and residences alike, [they are well-arranged].
Those whose intellects are fixed on the construction of joints and fortifications; those in taverns and liquor shops;
and those in slaughterhouses, rice-houses, and brothel houses.
See the courtesans and the harlots fashioned upon the gem;
and the garland-makers and the dyers.
To the perfumer, the draper,
the goldsmith, and the jeweler—
behold what is fashioned within the gem.
To cooks and kitchen-stewards,
to actors, dancers, and singers,
to hand-clappers and water-carriers,
Behold what is fashioned within the gem.
Behold the kettledrums and tabors,
the conchs, the cymbals, and the drums.
And all the percussion instruments,
see them fashioned upon the jewel;
as well as the *saṃmatāla* drum and the lute.
Behold, upon the gem, the dancing, singing, and beautiful instrumental music, resounded by cymbals and drums, all fashioned there.
There were also acrobats, boxers,
illusionists, and Sobhiyas;
as well as corpse-revivers and wrestlers.
Behold what is fashioned within this jewel:
here, assemblies proceed,
crowded with men and women.
Beds upon beds, and floors;
behold what is fashioned upon the gem.
Behold the Mallas at their festival.
See the double arm being struck,
and when it is struck down,
see the image fashioned within the gem.
Behold, at the foot of the mountains,
many herds of various wild animals:
lions, tigers, and boars.
Hyenas, brown bears, and raccoons;
gavayas, wild oxen, red deer, and ruru deer;
palāsāda birds and gavajas; buffaloes, rohit deer, and ruru deer.
There were black antelopes and boars,
herds of wild pigs,
and many variegated kadalimigas.
Cats and porcupines,
and various herds of wild beasts—
behold them fashioned within the jewel.
The rivers have beautiful banks,
strewn with golden sands;
they flow with clear waters.
It is frequented by schools of fish;
and here there are crocodiles, sea-monsters, sharks, and turtles.
Pāṭhīna fish, pāvusa fish,
balaja, muñja, and rohita—
swarming with various flocks of birds.
Filled with various multitudes of trees,
look at the image fashioned within the jewel from the Veḷuriya River.
Behold these lotus ponds,
well-apportioned in the four directions,
teeming with flocks of various birds.
Frequented by various creatures,
the earth— with its oceans for earrings— is endowed with water on all sides.
Surrounded by rows of forests,
behold it fashioned from jewels;
look ahead at Videha.
Behold, O Goyānīya, behind me,
the land of Kuru and Jambudīpa fashioned upon this gem.
Behold the moon and the sun,
illuminating the four quarters as they revolve around Sineru.
Behold what is fashioned within the jewel:
Mount Sineru and the Himālayas,
the ocean and the surface of the earth.
And see the Four Great Kings fashioned upon the jewel,
as well as in the parks and forest groves.
And on the rocky mountain slope,
delightful and crowded with kimpurisas,
behold what is fashioned upon the gem.
The Phārusaka grove, the Cittalata grove,
the Missaka grove, the Nandana grove,
and the Vejayanta palace.
Behold what is fashioned within the jewel:
Sudhamma, Tāvatiṃsa,
and the blossoming Pāricchattaka tree.
Behold Erāvaṇa, the king of nāgas,
fashioned within the gem. Behold there the celestial maidens.
Like lightning flashing in the sky,
as they wander through Nandana,
behold them fashioned within the jewel.
Behold these celestial maidens,
who entice the sons of the gods, as they take delight with the sons of the gods.
Behold what is fashioned within the gem:
a palace more than a thousand fathoms high,
its floor strewn with beryl fruit.
And see the forms fashioned within the blazing gem;
[the realms of] the Thirty-three and Yāma.
And also in Tusita, in Nimmāna,
and among the Paranimmitavasavatti gods—
behold what is fashioned upon the gem.
Behold these lotus ponds,
pure with their serene waters,
covered with mandārava flowers.
And with lotuses and water-lilies.
Therein, ten lines are white,
and ten blue, most enchanting.
Six were tawny, fifteen were turmeric-colored,
and fourteen were yellow;
twenty among them were golden.
Twenty made of silver;
thirty are seen with the luster of the color of an *indagopaka* insect.
Therein, ten were Kāḷiyas and six Mañjeṭṭhās;
twenty-five were mixed with Bandhuka flowers.
Variegated with blue lotuses.
Thus, endowed with every limb,
radiant and luminous;
"Behold, O Great King, best of bipeds, the Odhisuṅka,
known as Maṇikaṇḍa."
3. The Chapter on the Collar-Bone “O King, approach and examine this mark;
you do not possess such a jewel-treasure as this.”
Let us win by righteousness and without violence;
if you have won, declare it quickly.
O Pañcāla, Paccuggata, Sūrasena!
Let the Macchas, the Maddas,
and the Kekakas behold this battle fought by one free from deceit;
they do not do anything at all in our assembly hall.
Intoxicated by the pride of their own invincibility, they entered:
the King of the Kurus, the Yakkha Puṇṇaka,
and the King Kali, who took his turn at the dice.
A yakkha named Puṇṇaka took up the dice.
There, both of them met at the game of dice in the presence of kings and in the midst of friends.
When Ajēsi the yakkha [attacked] the best of men, a tumultuous clamor arose there:
"Victory, O Great King! And defeat!"
“Success has come to one of them;
O Lord of Men, you live by means of excellent wealth.
Since I have been defeated, please restore it to me quickly.”
“Elephants, cattle, horses, and jeweled earrings, as well as whatever treasure I possess on earth—
take from me, Kaccāna, the best of riches.”
“Take these and go wherever you wish.
“Elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings,
and whatever treasure else you have upon this earth— ”
“The best among them was named Vidhura, the creator;
he has been won by me—explain that to me.
“He is my very self, my refuge, and my goal.”
He is my island, my shelter, and my final refuge;
he is not to be weighed against my wealth,
for this doer is equal to my very life.
“Long has there been dispute between me and you;
let us go to him and ask him himself.
Let him alone explain this matter to us.”
“Let there be conversation between us both.
“Surely you speak the truth,
and you have not acted rashly, young man.”
"Let us go to him and ask;
by that we both shall be satisfied.
"Do the gods truly know this of the Kurus?"
A minister named Vidhura, established in the Dhamma—
were you a slave to the king, or were you a kinsman?
By what means did you come to be known as "Vidhura" in the world?
“Some become slaves by birthright,
some become slaves purchased with wealth;
and some even enter into slavery of their own accord.”
Even those driven by fear become slaves.
These four indeed are the slaves of men;
for truly, I too am born from a womb.
Whether there be a king or no king,
even after going to another world,
O youth, let him give me to you according to the Dhamma.
“This is my second victory today;
for when asked, the questioner has revealed the answer.
Alas, this best of kings is indeed one whose form is unrighteous!”
"You do not acknowledge my well-spoken words.
"If he had opened up this question to us in this way:
'I am a slave, and I am certainly not a kinsman'..."
“Take, Kaccāna, a boon of wealth;
having taken it, go wherever you wish.
This is the section on the collarbone.
4. The Question on Household Life “Vidhura,
for a householder living in his own home, [what is the difficulty?]”
What would his mode of livelihood be?
How indeed would there be his gathering [of requisites]?
How would it be free from harm?
And how does a youth who speaks the truth,
having passed from this world to the next, not grieve?
One who possesses understanding therein, fortitude,
intelligence, and insight into the goal;
one who has fully analyzed all phenomena—
Vidhura said this:
“I am not one whose wife is shared with others,
nor do I eat delicious food alone.”
One should not serve a materialist;
this does not lead to the increase of wisdom.
One who is virtuous and perfected in conduct—
Diligent and discerning,
humble in conduct, free from arrogance,
gentle, amiable, and mild.
One who gathers friends through acts of kindness,
who shares and is well-ordered,
should satisfy them with food and drink.
One should always [be devoted] to recluses and brahmins;
one should be a lover of the Dhamma,
a retainer of what has been heard, and an inquirer.
One should attend with reverence upon those who are virtuous and learned,
even while living as a householder.
For a householder, his own home is [his refuge];
thus his livelihood may be secure,
and thus indeed there is his support.
Thus may there be freedom from ill will,
and the young man shall be a speaker of truth;
[passing] from this world to the next world...
Thus, having passed away, one does not grieve.
This concludes the "Questions on the Householder's Life.
Section 5: Characteristics.
“Come now, let us go;
I have been given to you by the Lord.
Attend to my welfare alone.”
“This is the eternal law.
“I know you, young man;
I have been given to you by my master.”
"And let us have you stay in our home for three days, so that we may soon instruct our sons.
"Let it be so for me; let us stay for three days."
Perform today the duties within the household;
instruct your children and wife today,
so that you may be happy after passing away.”
Having said, “So be it,” the yakkha, full of desire,
departed together with Vidhura;
he followed that [chariot] drawn by noble elephants and horses.
The most noble of men entered the inner palace;
there he approached the lovely, divine, and beautiful forms of the krauñca bird, the peacock, and the beloved ketaka flower.
Abounding in food and plentiful in drink,
like Masakkasāra belongs to Vāsava;
there they dance and sing.
They call out to him, the superior among the superior,
like well-adorned women among the gods, like celestial nymphs.
Having provided the yakkha with young women,
food, and drink, Dhammapāla reflected upon his own various goals.
Then he approached his wife.
She was anointed with the scent and essence of sandalwood,
resembling refined gold from the Jambu river.
Her husband spoke to his wife: "Come, lady, listen!
Address your sons, O tawny-eyed one.
Having heard her husband's words, she did not disregard them.
“Address the daughter-in-law with copper-colored nails and beautiful eyes;
call these two who wear lovely garments—
sons whose names are like the blue lotus flower.”
When they had arrived at his head, Dhammapāla,
without wavering, kissed his sons and,
having addressed them, spoke these words:
“I have been given here by the king to this young man. Now,
happy in myself and subject to his will,
I shall take him and go wherever he desires.”
And I have come to instruct you;
how could I depart without protecting you?
If the King who dwells in the Kuru realm [should come] to you...
Janasandha, desiring much, would ask:
"What do you know from of old? What did your father instruct you in the past?"
All of you, come together with me;
for who here is a man more intimate to the king than I?
Therefore, making this gesture of reverence, speak thus:
"Do not say so, O King, for this is not right;
how could a seat of equal height belong to a king of tigers who is of low birth?"
The Section on Characteristics.
6. Royal Residence.
And he [bestowed] upon his sons and ministers...
To his kinsmen and well-wishers,
Vidhura, with a mind free from dejection, spoke these words.
“Sisters, having sat down in the royal residence,
listen to me as to how one who has entered a royal family [should conduct himself].”
A person incurs disgrace;
for one who has entered a royal court does not obtain renown if he remains unknown.
Neither a coward nor one of dull wit,
never heedless at any time;
when his virtue and wisdom—
He attains purity,
and then he places his trust in me,
not concealing his secrets from me.
Just as a scale, when properly held and well-balanced with equal arms,
does not waver when questioned.
He dwelt in the king's service.
Just as a scale that is held up is well-balanced and properly maintained with equal arms;
Overcoming all [these],
he lived in the king’s service,
whether by day or by night.
Wise in royal affairs,
he should not waver when summoned;
such a one may dwell in the king’s service.
Whether by day or by night,
the wise man, accomplishing all his royal duties, [remains steadfast].
He dwelt in the king’s residence.
And whatever path was well-prepared for him,
well-laid out by the king;
One should not go where one is spoken to by him;
one should live under the king's authority.
One should not eat what is equal to the king's.
Never indulging in sensual pleasures,
he would follow behind everyone everywhere;
such a person lives under the king’s authority.
There is no cloth like that of a king,
nor garland, nor ointment;
nor his deportment or his dignified bearing.
One should not act like a king;
one should adopt a different demeanor if one is to dwell in a king's service.
The king played with his ministers,
surrounded by his wives;
yet no minister was among the king's wives.
A wise person should cultivate this state:
undisturbed, not fickle,
prudent, with senses restrained.
Endowed with a noble mental aspiration,
he dwelt in the king’s residence;
he did not dally with the wives of others.
He should not consult in secret;
he should not take wealth from the king's treasury;
such a person may dwell in the king’s service.
One should not prize sleep,
nor drink liquor for intoxication;
one should not kill deer in the forest.
He dwelt in the king’s residence.
For him there was no chair, no couch,
no stool, no boat, and no chariot.
Thinking, "I am esteemed," he enters the royal residence and dwells there;
he should keep himself not too far from the king.
Neither too close nor too far,
the discerning one should stand facing him,
visible to his master.
A king is certainly not a friend,
nor is a king a partner for sexual union;
kings become angry quickly.
Like a pig’s eye that has been struck,
the wise and intelligent person does not think, "I have been honored."
One should answer harshly even when addressed by a king in his assembly;
having gained an opening, one should secure that opening.
One should not place trust even in kings;
like fire, one should remain self-restrained while living under the rule of a king.
A kshatriya may seize his son or his brother by force,
along with their villages or market towns.
Whether from kingdoms or from provinces,
one should remain silent and equanimous,
not speaking words that are clever yet wicked.
To those elephant-riders in the army,
to the charioteers and the foot-soldiers—
by their declaration of their deeds, [they are known].
The king increases their wages;
one should not go between them,
but dwell in that royal residence.
A wise man, even if he has a belly as large as a bow,
may cause a bamboo to tremble;
yet he would not act in a contrary manner.
He dwelt in the king’s residence.
His belly was as thin as a bowstring;
he was like a fish that has no tongue for its livelihood.
One who is frugal, prudent,
and brave may dwell in the king’s service;
he should not engage excessively with women.
Perceiving the exhaustion of his vital heat,
one whose wisdom is spent falls victim to coughing, asthma, colic, and weakness.
One should not speak excessively,
nor should one always remain silent;
one’s speech should be unscattered and measured.
One should speak at the proper time.
Free from anger, without conflict,
truthful, gentle, and free from backbiting;
One should not speak deceptive words;
such a person may dwell in the royal palace.
One should be a supporter of one’s mother and father.
One who honors the elders in the family,
who is gentle and speaks with courtesy,
may dwell in the royal residence.
Trained, skilled in arts, tamed,
self-controlled, disciplined, gentle,
heedful, pure, and clever.
He lived in the king’s residence,
humble in conduct toward the elders,
respectful and reverent.
One who is self-controlled is pleasant to dwell with;
such a person may live in the royal residence.
One should avoid [the opposite] from afar.
One should look only to one's own husband for support, even when people are sent together,
and not to another king.
One should respectfully attend upon ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous and learned.
He dwelt in the king’s residence,
as well as among recluses and brahmins who were virtuous and learned.
One should attend upon them with reverence;
such a person dwells in the residence of kings,
as well as among recluses and brahmins.
One who is virtuous and learned should satisfy them with food and drink;
such a person may dwell in the king’s service.
One should attend upon and serve those who possess wisdom— whether they be ascetics or brahmins— who are virtuous and learned.
Desiring one's own growth,
one should not neglect the giving previously bestowed upon recluses and brahmins.
He would not hinder anyone at the time of giving to those seeking alms—
one who is wise and endowed with intelligence.
Skilled in the methods of ritual procedure,
knowing the right time and knowing the proper occasion—
he may dwell in the king's residence.
One who is industrious in their field of action,
heedful and discerning,
with well-ordered tasks—
He dwells in the king’s residence;
he goes constantly to the threshing floor, the sal grove, the cattle pen, and the field.
One should store grain in moderation,
and likewise cook food in moderation in the house;
one should treat a son or a brother with restraint.
Those who are not established in virtue are indeed bodiless fools;
they are just like the departed spirits.
While they were sitting,
he caused them to be served food and alms;
[he provided] slaves, laborers, and messengers.
Well-composed in his virtues,
